extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in classical geometry, conic sections, and curve theory (readers of 19th-century mathematical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of classical-geometry problems, lemmas, and constructive methods (inscribing polygons in circles, properties of conics and higher-order curves, loci of midpoints, and related analytic criteria), with worked solutions and remarks on method applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction by successive parallels for inscribing polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe a polygon with given angles in a circle: from a chosen point M draw MR parallel to a given side AB, join ROH, then through successive vertices draw parallels (e.g., MR, RS, ST, TU, ...) and join corresponding points (ROH, SPK, TQX, UMY, EXY, etc.) to form the polygon IRSTU etc.; the constructed polygon's angles (MRS, RST, STU, ...) will respectively equal given angles (AHK, HKX, KXY, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parity of the number of sides determines the final determination step: if the figure to be inscribed has an odd number of sides (so the constructed polygon has even number of right lines), the whole arc MRSTU ... will be given and hence UM (the subtending chord) and the initial point M are determined. If the figure has an even number of sides the argument uses parity of the right lines and parallel relations (produce YMU to F so angle FFA is given), yielding M. Q.E.D. — use the parity rule to know which auxiliary arc/angle fixes M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma I — two given points, third side parallel to a given line
rubrics_metrics.description: Through two given points to draw lines meeting in the circumference of a given circle so that the line joining the other intersections with the circle shall be parallel to a given line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: inscribe a triangle in a given circle with two sides passing through given points and whose third side is parallel to a given line. The text notes this is 'too simple to need further remark' — treat as a base construction used in reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II — inscribing triangle through three given points
rubrics_metrics.description: Through two given points to inflect (i.e. direct) lines to a point in the circumference of a given circle so that they shall contain a given ... (used to inscribe a triangle in a circle whose sides pass through three given points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis reduces the problem to Lemma I; the construction essentially coincides with Ottajano's general solution adapted to this special case. Use as the principal tool when the problem requires sides through given points (particularly for even-sided cases as noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction strategy for n‑gon inscribed in a circle (Fuss/Ottajano/Malfatti approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: General method: reduce problems of inscribing polygons with sides parallel to given lines or passing through given points, case by case, to the previously solved lemmas; when number of given sides is odd the solution depends on Lemma I, when even on Lemma II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply successive reductions: e.g., join certain given points, draw chords parallel to these joins, use intersections with secants and tangent‑square relations to identify further required points; the 'invariable method' handles points inside or outside the circle and resolves indeterminate cases with parity-aware adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tangent‑square = rectangle of secant segments to locate points
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructions where secants and chords are drawn from exterior points meeting the circle, rectangles of intercepts (e.g., AB·BP or PC·Q) equal the square of the tangent drawn from that exterior point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method repeatedly uses the identity 'rectangle = square of tangent' to determine points (e.g., P, Q, R, ... are 'given' once AB·BP equals the square of tangent from B). Use this relation to compute or construct intersection points when joining given external points to the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lhuilier's case breakdown for inscribing a triangle in a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the triangle-inscription problem into four cases: (1) The three sides parallel to given lines; (2) Two sides parallel to given lines, the third through a given point; (3) One side parallel to a given line, the other two through given points; (4) All sides through given points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case is analysed successively and reduced to antecedent cases; treat the list as a decision tree to choose the appropriate reduction/construction routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lhuilier's case breakdown for inscribing a quadrilateral in a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the quadrilateral-inscription problem into five cases: (1) Four sides parallel to given lines; (2) Three sides parallel to given lines, the fourth through a given point; (3) Two sides parallel to given lines, the other two through given points; (4) One side parallel to a given line, the other three through given points; (5) All sides through given points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce cases in succession to earlier ones where possible; note special indeterminate/determinate subcases (e.g., when given points lie within the circle) that require separate attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity rule (General Scholium) for choice of lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of given sides being odd, the solution depends on the first lemma; being even, on the second. This rule remains valid if some given points lie within the given circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parity (odd/even count of given sides) to choose between analytical tracks (Lemma I or II). It gives a uniform approach to the general problem of inscribing polygons with mixed constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Morgan theorem on central conjugates and polars (constructive criterion for conics)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two lines (intersecting in O) are drawn in the plane of a second‑order curve, and if the central conjugate of each line be drawn and produced to meet the other in points B and B', then BB' is parallel to the polar line of O. Conversely, choosing axes through O and points B (on one axis) and B' (on the other), and taking the polar line of O parallel to BB', determines one and only one conic of the second order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a practical way to construct or identify a conic from three conjugate lines/points plus a polar direction; it gives geometric meaning to certain coefficient relations of the general second‑degree equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of vanishing coefficients and reference to conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the general second‑degree form degenerates (e.g., a f x^2 + c y^2 + f = 0 with certain coefficients zero), a vanishing coefficient corresponds to the polar of the origin being at infinite distance (origin at the centre), or to the axes being conjugate diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate algebraic vanishing of coefficients into geometric statements about the position of the origin relative to the conic (centre, conjugate diameters), and note the corresponding indeterminacies of B, B' in the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for distinguishing parabola/ellipse/hyperbola by positional signs
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of b^2 − 4ac (and related sign patterns of quantities associated with points A, C, B, B') agrees with geometric placement: if among the four points A, C, B, B' three lie on boundary of one pair of opposite axis‑angles and one on the other, the curve is a hyperbola; other distributions allow ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola. If AB' and CB are parallel, the curve is a parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret movement of B' (relative to B) while keeping B fixed to determine whether the conic is ellipse (B' must be moved away from origin), hyperbola (B' moved towards origin), or parabola (BC || AB'). Use this to classify a conic from geometric data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and first method for diameters of a curve (locus of midpoints of parallel chords)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a diameter of a plane curve as the locus of middle points of a series of parallel chords. Method 1: Write equation of chord y = p x + q (p fixed), denote roots/abscissae of intersection points and use root relations (if x1,x2 are abscissae then x1 + x2 = 2x_mid) to eliminate parameters and derive the locus equation (apply to 2nd and 3rd order curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply elimination between the curve equation and chord equation, use relations between roots to express the middle point coordinates and eliminate chord parameters p,q to obtain the diameter's equation. Works well for 2nd and 3rd order curves; leads generally to a curve of comparable order (e.g., third order gives diameters of third order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second method for diameters via origin translation and symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Method 2: Transform coordinates so that the origin is at the midpoint of an arbitrary chord; then the chord endpoints acquire equal and opposite coordinates. Impose that the transformed curve equation in (x,y) contains only even powers in x (so the two symmetric roots are ±), leading to algebraic remainder conditions whose elimination yields the diameter equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is applicable to all curves in principle and is often algebraically simpler for low-degree curves: equate remainders and demand vanishing of certain coefficients (see equations (14) in text). Yields explicit relations between midpoint coordinates (h,k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree/result expectations for diameters of low‑order curves
rubrics_metrics.description: For curves of the second and third order, the described methods yield diameter equations; for a general third‑order curve the diameter is itself generally a curve of the same (third) order. In examples (e.g., certain polynomial curves) the resulting diameter equation may be of higher degree (the example given yields a sixth‑order equation for a specific family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate degree growth when applying the algebraic elimination; use symmetry and factor-division to simplify where possible. Note: the first method may not extend straightforwardly to higher orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limitation of the root‑based diameter method
rubrics_metrics.description: The root‑sum method (using relations like x1 + x2 = 2x_mid and elimination of chord parameters) applies to curves of second and third degree, but 'not (it would seem) to those of higher orders.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the origin‑translation symmetry method for very high order curves; for 2nd/3rd degree the root method is efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature/surface tangent‑plane sign criterion (second derivative test for surfaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a surface F(x,y,z)=0, form the quadratic form built from second partial derivatives (the Hessian-like expression given). If the expression is positive at a point, the surface near that point lies entirely on one side of the tangent plane; if negative, the surface lies partly on each side; if zero the section is a parabola (or two parallel lines) and one principal radius of curvature is infinite (developable surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute second partials and substitute into the indicated expression (analogue of discriminant). Use sign to classify local surface geometry relative to tangent plane. Note: criterion holds for rectangular or oblique axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector/force representation theorem for triangle centers
rubrics_metrics.description: If lines drawn from one of the centres of the escribed circles of a plane triangle or from the centre of the inscribed circle to the other three represent in magnitude and direction three forces, then the line joining this centre and that of the circumscribing circle represents in magnitude and direction one fourth of the resultant; in particular, the four forces represented by lines from circumcenter to in/excenters are in equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decomposition into diameters (bisectors) and symmetry: pairwise equal/opposite components cancel leading to equilibrium results and center-of-gravity conclusions (centre of gravity of equal bodies at in/excenters coincides with circumcenter). Useful for force‑analytic or barycentric arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction for chord with given rectangle-of-segments (CXLI/ CXLI I problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a given point P on circumference of circle to draw a chord intersecting two sides of a given inscribed triangle so that the rectangle of its extreme segments equals a given square: construct PB, make circumference PT equal to circumference PA, draw TO parallel to PB and choose TO so PB·TO equals the given square; join PO and describe appropriate arc to intersect AC in R then draw PQRS giving the required chord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution hinges on creating a parallelogram and using similarity of triangles (PQB similar to RSN) so that the rectangle PQ·RS equals PB·OT (constructed) — use parallels and equal arc construction as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximizing visible spherical surface from a point on a circle between two sphere centres (CXLI II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two spheres radii r1,r2 with centres at ends of a line 2a and a circle described on that as diameter, find point on circumference from which greatest portion of spherical surfaces is visible: set distances from centres X and Y and use surface‑segment formulas leading to equations (1),(2); extremize sum via differentiation to obtain distances x = (2 a r1^2)/(r1^2 + r2^2)^{1/2}(r1 + r2)?? (text gives explicit formulas for x and y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple solutions provided: calculus (substitute and differentiate to extremize sum), geometric trigonometric reduction (use cos/sin expressions), or algebraic manipulation of segment heights. Use the provided formulas for the distances producing maximum visible area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial parallelogram/trigonometry identity (AC cos CAX decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parallelogram ABCD in space, with diagonal AC and an arbitrary line AX through A, show by plane trigonometry that AC·cos(CAX) = AB·cos(BAX) + AD·cos(DAX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two solution approaches: project perpendiculars to AX and use right triangles/parallel projections; or use vector/coordinate relations via squared distances and right-angle properties. This is a constructive identity for decomposing the projected length of a diagonal into projections of adjacent sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola harmonic‑mean property (CXLV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given AB as hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle ADB and a parabola described about triangle having vertex at D, through C (a point on AB) draw CH perpendicular to AB meeting the parabola in H; then CH is a harmonic mean between AC and CB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple proofs: using standard parabola chord properties (EA:EC::ED:ED−CH), segment-height relations, or bisection and Hutton's property. Use these parabola ratios to derive CH as harmonic mean of AC and CB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic progression property from triangle side‑square progression
rubrics_metrics.description: If the squares of the sides of a triangle are in arithmetical progression, then the lines drawn from the angles to a point within the triangle so as to make equal angles with each other are in arithmetical progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the equal angle condition (120° between each pair) to write cosine relations among squared lengths (expressed as sums with −2·product·cos120°) and reduce by the arithmetic progression hypothesis to algebraic relations proving x,y,z are in arithmetic progression; handle equilateral special case separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus problem introduced — midpoints of equal chords in an ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem introduced: 'Find the locus of the middle points of equal chords in an ellipse' (beginning of solution announced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text proceeds to set the equation of the ellipse and begins analytic solution (not fully contained in chunk). Treat as a standard analytic-locus exercise: fix chord length, parametrize chords with slope p, set equal chord condition and eliminate parameters to get locus equation.
